style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive prose) + amplified study form; em-dashes used sparingly; narrative register

1.text: Now Naomi had a relative on her husband's side — a man of standing and substance, from the family of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz.
1.amp: ...a man of great worth [gibbor chayil -- a man mighty in wealth, character, and standing], of the family of Elimelech, named Boaz.
1.notes: gibbor chayil (H1368/H2428) = a man of valor and substance -- the very phrase used of warriors, here of his worth and means. The narrator quietly plants the kinsman who can rescue them before Ruth ever meets him.

2.text: Ruth the Moabitess said to Naomi, "Let me go out to the fields and glean among the ears of grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor." And Naomi said to her, "Go, my daughter."
2.notes: laqat (H3950) = to glean. The law commanded landowners to leave the field's edges and dropped grain for the poor, the widow, and the foreigner (Lev. 19:9-10; Deut. 24:19) -- Ruth, who is all three, throws herself on God's provision through His law.

3.text: So she went out, and came and gleaned in the field behind the reapers; and as it happened, she came to the portion of the field belonging to Boaz, who was of the family of Elimelech.
3.amp: ...and her chance brought her [qarah -- 'as it happened' -- to the human eye, mere chance] to the part of the field belonging to Boaz.
3.notes: qarah (H7136) = to happen/chance upon. The narrator's wink: it looks like luck, but the whole book is showing the unseen hand of the LORD steering every 'chance' to its appointed end.

4.text: Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and said to the reapers, "The LORD be with you." And they answered him, "The LORD bless you."
4.notes: A small window into Boaz's house: master and workers bless one another in the name of the LORD -- the everyday piety of a godly man.

5.text: Then Boaz said to his servant who was set over the reapers, "Whose young woman is this?"

6.text: The servant in charge of the reapers answered, "She is the Moabite girl who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab.

7.text: She said, 'Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves behind the reapers.' So she came, and she has kept at it from morning until now, resting only a little in the shelter."
7.notes: Ruth asks permission even for what the law already grants her, and works without pause -- her diligence and humility are noticed before her name is even known.

8.text: Then Boaz said to Ruth, "Listen, my daughter. Do not go to glean in another field; do not leave this one, but stay close here beside my young women.
8.notes: Boaz moves at once from permission to protection, folding the foreign widow into the safety of his own household.

9.text: Keep your eyes on the field they are reaping, and follow along after them. Have I not ordered the young men not to touch you? And when you are thirsty, go to the jars and drink from what the young men have drawn."
9.notes: naga (H5060) = to touch/harm. A lone foreign woman in the fields was vulnerable; Boaz commands her safety and her thirst's relief -- grace beyond the letter of the law.

10.text: Then she fell on her face, bowing to the ground, and said to him, "Why have I found such favor in your eyes, that you would take notice of me — and I only a foreigner?"
10.amp: Why have I found favor in your eyes [chen -- undeserved grace] that you would notice me [nakar -- single me out, acknowledge me], a foreigner [nokri -- a stranger, the very root of the word for 'notice']?
10.notes: chen (H2580) = grace/favor; nakar (H5234) = to recognize/regard; nokri (H5237) = foreigner. There is a deliberate echo: the foreigner (nokri) is recognized (nakar) -- the outsider is seen and welcomed. Ruth marvels at grace she has not earned.

11.text: Boaz answered her, "It has been fully told to me — all that you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband: how you left your father and mother and the land of your birth, and came to a people you did not know before.
11.notes: Boaz recounts Ruth's faith in terms that echo Abraham's call (Gen. 12:1) -- she too left family and homeland to come to the people and God of the promise.

12.text: May the LORD repay your deed, and may a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge."
12.amp: ...under whose wings [kanaph -- the spread wing of a mother bird, and the corner of a garment drawn protectively over another] you have come to take refuge [chasah -- to seek shelter].
12.notes: kanaph (H3671) = wing / skirt-corner; chasah (H2620) = to take refuge. Boaz's blessing becomes the book's hinge: he prays that Ruth find shelter under the LORD's wings -- and in 3:9 Ruth will ask Boaz to spread his own 'wing' over her, making him the very answer to his prayer.

13.text: And she said, "Let me keep finding favor in your eyes, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken to the heart of your servant — though I am not even one of your servant women."
13.amp: ...you have spoken to the heart [dibber al-leb -- spoken tenderly, to the very heart] of your servant, though I am not as one of your servant women.
13.notes: dibber al-leb (H1696/H3820) = to speak to the heart -- words of comfort and kindness. Ruth marvels that she is treated above her station, an outsider spoken to as kin.

14.text: At mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come over here, eat some bread, and dip your morsel in the sour wine." So she sat beside the reapers, and he passed her roasted grain. She ate and was satisfied, and had some left over.
14.notes: Boaz seats the foreign gleaner at his own table among the workers, and gives so generously that the once-empty woman now has more than enough -- a quiet foretaste of fullness reversing the emptiness of chapter 1.

15.text: When she rose to glean, Boaz ordered his young men, "Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not shame her.
15.notes: kalam (H3637) = to humiliate/shame. Boaz lets Ruth glean even where it is not customary, and forbids any insult -- dignity guarded along with provision.

16.text: And even pull out some stalks for her from the bundles on purpose, and leave them for her to glean — and do not rebuke her."
16.notes: Boaz commands a hidden, deliberate generosity: grain 'accidentally' dropped so Ruth's gleaning will be abundant. Grace arranged to look like good fortune.

17.text: So she gleaned in the field until evening, and then beat out what she had gathered — and it came to about an ephah of barley.
17.amp: ...about an ephah of barley [roughly 30 pounds -- an astonishing yield for a single day's gleaning].
17.notes: An ephah (H374) ≈ 22 liters / ~30 lbs of grain: many days' food, far beyond a normal gleaning. Boaz's hidden kindness shows in the size of the harvest she carries home.

18.text: She took it up and went into the town, and her mother-in-law saw how much she had gleaned. Ruth also brought out and gave her what she had left over after she was satisfied.
18.notes: Ruth returns laden, and shares even her leftovers with Naomi -- the daughter-in-law who 'cleaved' to her is now her provider.

19.text: Her mother-in-law said to her, "Where did you glean today? Where did you work? Blessed be the man who took notice of you." So she told her mother-in-law with whom she had worked: "The name of the man I worked with today is Boaz."
19.notes: Naomi, who came home calling herself 'empty,' now pronounces a blessing -- the first sign of hope reviving in her. Then the name lands: Boaz.

20.text: Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "May he be blessed by the LORD, whose covenant kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead." And Naomi added, "The man is a close relative of ours — one of our kinsman-redeemers."
20.amp: ...the LORD, whose kindness [hesed -- loyal covenant love] has not abandoned the living or the dead... the man is one of our redeemers [go'el -- the near kinsman with the right and duty to redeem].
20.notes: hesed (H2617) again -- Naomi at last sees the LORD's faithfulness breaking through her bitterness. go'el (H1350) = the kinsman-redeemer who buys back a relative's land, marries a widow to raise an heir, and avenges blood (Lev. 25:25, 47-49). The whole plot now turns on this one word: Boaz can redeem them.

21.text: Ruth the Moabitess said, "He even told me, 'Stay close by my young workers until they have finished all my harvest.'"

22.text: And Naomi said to Ruth her daughter-in-law, "It is good, my daughter, that you go out with his young women, so that no one may harm you in another field."

23.text: Ruth held fast, then, beside Boaz's young women, gathering grain until both the barley harvest and the wheat harvest were finished; and all that while her home was with her mother-in-law.
23.notes: She 'held fast' (dabaq, H1692) -- the same clinging she pledged to Naomi in 1:14. The harvests pass, Ruth safe and provided for in Boaz's fields, living faithfully with Naomi -- the stage set for redemption once the grain is in.
